## Context

Per the [OAuth scope drift RFC's pre-flight #2](https://github.com/PostHog/requests-for-comments-internal/blob/matt/oauth-scope-drift-rfc/engineering/2026-05-04-oauth-scope-drift.md), three of the 15 OAuth scope incidents in the last 90 days were drift between `posthog/scopes.py` and `ALLOWED_PROVISIONING_SCOPES` (surface 1↔4):

- [#54272](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/54272) — provisioned PATs created with empty scopes (completely unusable until `MCP_PRESET_SCOPES` was added)
- [#55755](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/55755) — direct auth-code path applied to all partners; missing scope-allowlist validation
- [#57509](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/57509) — wizard's PKCE flow needed `llm_gateway:read`, `dashboard:write`, `insight:write` (this session)

[#57526](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/issues/57526)'s subset test catches "non-grantable scope in the allowlist" but does NOT catch "grantable scope missing from the allowlist that the wizard / partner integrations need." That gap is what bit Insforge.

## Change

Add a new test in `ee/api/agentic_provisioning/test/test_scope_validation.py` (the file added in #57509):

```python
WIZARD_BARE_MINIMUM_SCOPES = {
    "user:read", "project:read", "query:read",
    "llm_gateway:read", "dashboard:write", "insight:write",
}

def test_provisioning_allowlist_grants_wizard_required_scopes():
    missing = WIZARD_BARE_MINIMUM_SCOPES - ALLOWED_PROVISIONING_SCOPES
    assert not missing, (
        f"Partner allowlist is missing scopes the wizard needs: {missing}. "
        f"Either add them to ALLOWED_PROVISIONING_SCOPES, or update WIZARD_BARE_MINIMUM_SCOPES "
        f"if the wizard no longer needs them."
    )
```

Pair this with the existing subset/superset/ground-truth tests in #57526 — together they form the per-surface invariant for partner-issued tokens.

## Why

A test that catches under-provisioning would have stopped the Insforge bug from ever reaching the customer. Cheap to maintain, fails CI clearly with the named scope.

## Tracking

## Context

Once #57529 ships RFC 6750 \`insufficient_scope\` challenges and #57528 confirms client behavior, MCP no longer needs to publish its own \`scopes_supported\`. The AS becomes the single source of truth. Linear/Notion/Cloudflare/Stripe already ship without it.

This is the architecture from [Matt's #56835 review comment](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/56835#issuecomment-3567005020):
> Better fix is probably dropping scopes_supported from the resource metadata entirely. RFC 9728 makes it optional, the MCP spec says clients must omit scope when it's absent, and Linear/Notion/Cloudflare/Stripe already ship without it. One list (the AS), no drift.

## Change

Drop \`scopes_supported: OAUTH_SCOPES_SUPPORTED\` from \`services/mcp/src/index.ts:243\`. Reframe the \`OAUTH_SCOPES_SUPPORTED completeness\` test in \`tool-filtering.test.ts\` to assert against the AS list (which the existing generated file already mirrors). Delete \`bin/build-mcp-oauth-scopes.py\` and \`services/mcp/src/lib/oauth-scopes.generated.ts\` once nothing else depends on them.

## Feature-flagged rollout

The field's presence is gated by a server-side flag:

\`\`\`ts
scopes_supported: SCOPES_SUPPORTED_PUBLISHED_FLAG
  ? OAUTH_SCOPES_SUPPORTED
  : undefined,
\`\`\`

(Filtered out of the JSON if undefined.) Default off in dev/preview, off in canary, then full. Allows fast rollback without a deploy if a real-world client breaks.

## Pre-conditions

- [ ] #57525 (Cache-Control) shipped — bounds stale-cache blast radius
- [ ] #57526 (invariant tests) shipped — guards drift in remaining hand-maintained subsets
- [ ] #57527 (runtime intersection) shipped — interim self-correcting publication for the Django↔MCP race
- [ ] #57528 (client matrix) results in — confirms which clients we're safe to switch on
- [ ] #57529 (RFC 6750 challenges) shipped — clients have a runtime path to discover scopes

## Why

Reaches the spec-clean architecture: AS is the only place \`scopes_supported\` is published. Any future PostHog resource server (partner SDKs, etc.) inherits \"don't publish\" by default. The drift class is killed across all surfaces.

## Acceptance

- \`scopes_supported\` field absent from MCP metadata response when flag is off
- Codegen (\`bin/build-mcp-oauth-scopes.py\`) and generated file deleted, completeness test reframed
- Feature flag wired in, defaulted off, documented rollout plan
- Post-rollout: 0 \`invalid_scope\` errors in MCP auth logs over 7-day window vs. baseline

## Tracking

payload.author: MattBro
payload.body:
## Context

Today PostHog's REST API rejects scope-protected requests with a bare \`HttpResponseForbidden\` and no information about what scope was missing. Specifically:

- \`OAuthAccessTokenAuthentication.authenticate_header()\` at \`posthog/auth.py:655-656\` returns just \`\"Bearer\"\` with no challenge parameters
- Django OAuth Toolkit's \`ProtectedResourceMixin.dispatch()\` returns plain \`HttpResponseForbidden()\` (no \`WWW-Authenticate\` header at all)

This is non-compliant with RFC 6750 § 3 (Bearer Token Usage). Spec-compliant OAuth clients can't discover what scope they need to re-request, which is what makes the \"drop scopes_supported, rely on runtime hints\" approach impossible today.

## Change

Update \`OAuthAccessTokenAuthentication\` (and any sibling resource-server authn classes) to:

1. On insufficient-scope rejection, return a \`WWW-Authenticate\` header in the form:
   \`Bearer realm=\"posthog\", error=\"insufficient_scope\", scope=\"<missing-scope-list>\", error_description=\"...\"\`
2. On invalid/expired token, return:
   \`Bearer realm=\"posthog\", error=\"invalid_token\", error_description=\"...\"\`
3. On missing token (not authenticated):
   \`Bearer realm=\"posthog\"\`

## Implementation notes

- The decorator pattern PostHog uses (\`@required_scopes\`) should populate the missing-scope list onto the response so the auth class can read it
- Make sure the header survives Cloudflare / Envoy / any downstream proxy (audit as part of #57528)
- Keep the existing API JSON body shape (don't break clients that rely on it) — \`WWW-Authenticate\` is supplementary

## Why

Today: any OAuth-driven client that doesn't pre-discover scopes from \`scopes_supported\` fails opaquely on scope mismatch with no recovery path.

After this: clients can implement spec-compliant runtime scope discovery. Required infrastructure for #57530 (drop \`scopes_supported\`).

## Acceptance

- All scope-protected endpoints return RFC 6750-compliant \`WWW-Authenticate\` on 401/403
- Test coverage for each error class (insufficient_scope, invalid_token, missing_token)
- A documented client-side recovery flow: receive 401 with \`scope=\"x:read\"\`, re-authorize requesting \`x:read\`, retry

## Tracking

Parent: #57524
Blocks: #57530
Project: https://github.com/orgs/PostHog/projects/194

payload.author: MattBro
payload.body:
## Context

Before we can drop \`scopes_supported\` from MCP's RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata response (#57530), we need to know how each MCP client behaves when the field is absent or partial. RFC 9728 § 7.2 says the field is RECOMMENDED, not required, but the MCP spec is silent on what clients MUST do when it's absent. Claude Code has a [history of RFC 9728 non-compliance](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-ai-mcp/issues/5).

Without empirical data, dropping the field is wishful thinking. With it, we know exactly which user populations the structural cleanup helps and which need a different solution.

## Test matrix

For each client, install the PostHog MCP server and observe behavior under three configurations:

| Config | What to vary |
|---|---|

payload.author: MattBro
payload.body:
## Context

Even with #56835's codegen aligning the AS and MCP scope lists, hand-maintained scope subsets (\`ALLOWED_PROVISIONING_SCOPES\`, future partner allowlists, project-secret-key allowlists) can still drift from the canonical \`posthog/scopes.py\`. The introspection bug that nearly shipped in #57509 is the most recent example.

Codegen prevents drift in the lists it generates. Tests prevent drift in the lists it can't generate (because they're policy decisions, not derivations).

## Three tests to add

### 1. Subset invariant (catches non-grantable scopes in allowlists)

\`\`\`python
def test_provisioning_allowlist_is_subset_of_grantable():
    grantable = set(get_oauth_scopes_supported())
    diff = ALLOWED_PROVISIONING_SCOPES - grantable
    assert not diff, f"Partner allowlist contains non-grantable scopes: {diff}"
\`\`\`

Catches: someone adds \`introspection\` (non-scope) or a typo to a partner allowlist. The introspection bug from #57509.

### 2. Superset invariant (catches under-provisioned tools)

\`\`\`python
# In services/mcp/tests, after dropping the scopes_supported republication
def test_every_tool_required_scope_is_grantable_by_as():
    grantable = set(OAUTH_SCOPES_FROM_AS)  # from generated file or runtime fetch
    for tool in getToolDefinitions():
        for scope in tool.required_scopes:
            assert scope in grantable, f"Tool {tool.name} requires non-grantable scope {scope}"
\`\`\`

Catches: someone adds a tool with a typo'd scope name, or a scope that exists in scopes.py but is filtered out of \`get_oauth_scopes_supported()\` (e.g. \`OAUTH_HIDDEN_SCOPE_OBJECTS\`). The llm_skill bug from #55300 if it had been written as a tool with that scope.

### 3. Ground-truth invariant (catches AS list itself being wrong)

\`\`\`python
def test_as_grantable_matches_decorator_usage():
    decorator_used_scopes = collect_all_scopes_from_required_scopes_decorators()
    grantable = set(get_oauth_scopes_supported())
    diff = decorator_used_scopes - grantable
    assert not diff, (
        f"Endpoints declare @required_scopes for scopes not in AS-grantable list: {diff}. "
        f"Either add the scope to scopes.py or remove the decorator."
    )
\`\`\`

Catches: AS list itself is incomplete (the SPOF concern). If code uses \`@required_scopes(\"foo:read\")\` but \`foo:read\` isn't in \`get_oauth_scopes_supported()\`, no token can ever access that endpoint via OAuth.

## Acceptance

- All three tests added (Python in posthog/, plus a Node test in services/mcp/tests for #2 once we have a path to the AS list there)
- Tests fail clearly with named offending scope, not just \"set mismatch\"
- Existing CI catches drift at PR time before merge

## Tracking

payload.body:
## Context

The MCP server's RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata response at \`services/mcp/src/index.ts:239-251\` returns a JSON body with no \`Cache-Control\` header set explicitly (relies on framework defaults). RFC 9728 has no caching guidance and most clients cache for hours-to-days. mcp-remote caches in \`~/.mcp-auth/\` until manually cleared.

Today this is fine because the response is stable. The moment we change anything (drop \`scopes_supported\`, intersect at runtime, etc.) any stale cache entry becomes a bug for that client until they clear it.

## Change

Add \`Cache-Control: public, max-age=300\` to the metadata response.

\`\`\`ts
// services/mcp/src/index.ts:248
headers: {
  'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  'Cache-Control': 'public, max-age=300',
},
\`\`\`

## Why

5-minute worst-case stale window instead of indefinite. Mandatory pre-work for any structural change to scope publication.

## Tracking

Project: https://github.com/orgs/PostHog/projects/194

payload.author: MattBro
payload.body:
## Context

PostHog has multiple parallel scope lists across services that must agree. Drift between any two breaks OAuth sign-in for spec-compliant clients with `?error=invalid_scope`.

Surfaces today:
1. `posthog/scopes.py` (canonical source)
2. AS metadata `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` (computed from #1)
3. MCP protected-resource metadata `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` (generated from #1 via #56835)
4. `ALLOWED_PROVISIONING_SCOPES` partner allowlist (hand-maintained)
5. Wizard OAuth scope list `setup-utils.ts:495` (hand-maintained, separate repo)
6. Frontend `APIScopeObject` Literal mirror (hand-maintained per `scopes.py` warning)

[#56835](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/56835) closed surface 1↔3. The remaining surfaces are still hand-maintained.

## Goal

Reach the architecture from #56835's review thread: **AS is the single source of truth for `scopes_supported`**. Resource servers (MCP, future partners) don't republish their own lists. Drift is structurally impossible across all surfaces.

## Approach

Three-layer defense, shipped incrementally:

1. **Detect drift at PR time** via invariant tests — bounds blast radius for everything else
2. **Self-correcting publication** via runtime intersection — eliminates the deploy-race window between Django and MCP
3. **Single source of truth** — drop `scopes_supported` from resource metadata once RFC 6750 challenge infrastructure exists across PostHog API

## Child issues

- [ ] cap stale-cache blast radius via Cache-Control on protected-resource metadata
- [ ] add subset / superset / ground-truth invariant tests for OAuth scope lists
- [ ] drop stale introspection from wizard interactive OAuth scope list (PostHog/wizard)
- [ ] runtime-intersect bundled scope list with AS-grantable at MCP cold start
- [ ] MCP-client compatibility matrix for scopes_supported absence and 401 challenges
- [ ] emit RFC 6750 insufficient_scope WWW-Authenticate challenges from PostHog REST API
- [ ] drop scopes_supported from RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata (feature-flagged)
- [ ] replace wizard hardcoded scope list with runtime fetch + intersection from AS metadata (PostHog/wizard)

## Related

- #56835 — generates MCP scope list from posthog/scopes.py (closes surface 1↔3)
- #56833 — removes introspection from MCP scopes list
- #55300 — llm_skill drift incident (still open)
- #55307 — drift tracking issue

Marketplace partners that want to show real-time usage to their users in their own UI need PostHog to submit projected period usage on a daily cadence. Today this is hardcoded for Vercel. ## Problem

Each marketplace partner needs PostHog to submit each finalized Stripe invoice to their billing API. Today this is hardcoded for Vercel. Generalize so any partner with `Customer.billing_provider` set gets routed through their `MarketplaceBillingProviderClient.submit_invoice()`.

## What needs to happen

1. **Dispatch on `Customer.billing_provider`** in the `invoice.finalized` Stripe webhook handler — route to that provider's client; fall back to PostHog's default (charge the card directly) when unset.
2. **Normalized invoice payload** — generic shape, lifted from Vercel's, that all providers receive:
   ```json
   {
     "externalId": "in_1ABC...",
     "invoiceDate": "...",
     "period": { "start": "...", "end": "..." },
     "items": [
       { "billingPlanId": "...", "name": "...", "price": "...", "quantity": 0, "units": "...", "total": "..." }
     ],
     "discounts": [...],
     "memo": "..."
   }
   ```
3. **Store `invoiceId`** returned by the partner on `Invoice.billing_provider_metadata` for reconciliation.
4. **Retry semantics** on partner-API outage — exponential backoff with dead-letter so we can replay manually.
5. **Generic test mode** — preserve Vercel's `{"test": {"validate": true, "result": "paid"}}` capability as part of the base contract so any partner can validate their integration without real charges.

payload.author: MattBro
payload.body:
## Problem

Partner platforms increasingly want to front the billing relationship for their users — they receive invoices and usage from PostHog, collect from their users on their own billing infrastructure, and pay PostHog out-of-band per the marketplace contract. This is the "Vercel for Platforms" pattern.

Vercel uses this model today via a one-off `VercelClient` in the billing service. As more partners ask for the same shape, we need to lift the Vercel-specific implementation into a generic `MarketplaceBillingProviderClient` abstraction so adding the next partner is config + a registration flag, not net-new infrastructure.

## Goal

A single `BillingProviderClient` shape any marketplace partner can plug into:

- Wire up via partner's CIMD registration (or admin) by setting `provisioning_billing_provider` on the OAuthApplication
- On `Customer` creation during agentic provisioning, stamp the right provider on the customer record (immutable, matches existing Vercel contract)
- Billing pipeline dispatches every per-customer invoice and usage submission through that provider's client

## Scope

- **Core abstraction** — extract `MarketplaceBillingProviderClient` base from `VercelClient`. Re-implement Vercel as an instance of the generic shape, no behavior change for Vercel.
- **Generic invoice submission webhook** — child issue, see sub-issues.
- **Generic usage submission webhook** — child issue, see sub-issues.
- **Provisioning-side wiring** — `provisioning_billing_provider: str = ""` field on `OAuthApplication`. Partner registration sets it. Customer creation reads it and stamps `Customer.billing_provider`.
- **`OrganizationIntegration`** — extensible `kind` so each new partner has a place to store auth credentials.

## Open architectural decision: auth scheme

The biggest unresolved call. PostHog needs to authenticate to the partner's API on every invoice/usage submission. Three reasonable shapes, all already in use somewhere in the PostHog integration ecosystem:

| Option | How it works | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. OAuth / Bearer** (Vercel today) | Partner issues access tokens at install time; PostHog stores them in `OrganizationIntegration` and refreshes as needed | Matches Vercel; partner stays in standard OAuth ergonomics | Heaviest install ceremony; partner has to host an OAuth server |
| **B. Long-lived API key** | Partner generates an API key in their admin, gives it to PostHog at provisioning-app registration time; key stored encrypted in `OrganizationIntegration` | Lightest lift on both sides; matches how most SaaS partners issue credentials | Key rotation has to be handled manually; no scope hierarchy |
| **C. HMAC outbound** | PostHog signs each request with a shared secret; partner verifies. Same shape as our inbound HMAC for Stripe-style provisioning | Cleanest replay/integrity story; constant-time verification on partner side; no token management | Partners that don't already speak HMAC have to build it |

**Initial lean:** B — long-lived API key — for the first new partner. Lowest lift, easy to rotate when needed, degrades cleanly to a slot future partners can fill in. Doesn't preclude offering A or C later as additional supported schemes per partner.

Tracking the decision here rather than splitting to its own issue because the answer determines a chunk of the base class API. Open to input.

## First concrete user

[Insforge](https://insforge.dev) — YC backend-as-a-service for AI coding agents (~25k devs). Met 2026-05-01. They want PostHog to feel native inside their platform with Insforge fronting the billing relationship. They'll be the first partner using the generic shape end-to-end. They want invoice + usage submission so they can show real-time usage in their own UI. Spec for the Insforge-specific surface is internal.

## Reference

- Existing Vercel client: `billing/billing_providers/clients/vercel.py`
- Existing Vercel formatter: `billing/billing_providers/formatters/vercel.py`
- `billing

payload.body:
### Summary

The hosted PostHog MCP `query-run` tool rejects **every** payload — including the exact shapes shown in [`tests/unit/query-run-schema.test.ts`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/master/services/mcp/tests/unit/query-run-schema.test.ts) — with an identical Zod discriminated-union failure. The unit test passes locally, so this is a runtime/deployment-level issue rather than a schema-source bug.

Possibly the same surface as #41164, #43757, and #38607, but the failure mode here is total — it isn't model-specific or strict-mode-specific. **Anthropic models hit it too**, contradicting the "works for OpenAI/Anthropic" claim in #43757.

### Repro (8 payloads, all fail identically)

Called the live MCP `query-run` with each of these from a Claude Code session over the standard remote-bridge transport:

| # | Payload (just `query`) |
|---|---|
| 1 | `{"kind":"HogQLQuery","query":"SELECT 1"}` |
| 2 | `{"kind":"HogQLQuery","query":"SELECT 1","filters":{}}` |
| 3 | `{"kind":"DataVisualizationNode","source":{"kind":"HogQLQuery","query":"SELECT 1"}}` |
| 4 | `{"kind":"InsightVizNode","source":{"kind":"TrendsQuery","series":[{"kind":"EventsNode","event":"$pageview","custom_name":"test"}]}}` |
| 5 | `{"kind":"InsightVizNode","source":{"kind":"TrendsQuery","series":[{"kind":"EventsNode","event":"\$pageview","custom_name":"test"}],"dateRange":{"date_from":"-1d"}}}` |
| 6 | `{"kind":"EventsQuery"}` (negative control) |
| 7 | `{"kind":"DataTableNode"}` (negative control) |
| 8 | `"SELECT 1"` (negative control) |

All 8 return the exact same error:

```json
{
  "code": "invalid_union",
  "errors": [],
  "note": "No matching discriminator",
  "discriminator": "kind",
  "path": ["query", "kind"]
}
```

Note even payload #8 — a plain string for `query` — produces an error path of `["query","kind"]`. A type-correct Zod validator would error at `query` (expected object, got string), not descend into `.kind`. That suggests the discriminator detection runs unconditionally before the shape check.

The empty `errors: []` array is the giveaway: in Zod v4 `discriminatedUnion`, an empty `errors` array with `note: "No matching discriminator"` means the runtime literal map is empty / mis-built, so no input value can ever match.

### Source pointers

- [`services/mcp/src/schema/tool-inputs.ts:393-401`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/master/services/mcp/src/schema/tool-inputs.ts#L393) — `QueryRunQuerySchema = z.discriminatedUnion('kind', [InsightVizNodeSchema, DataVisualizationNodeSchema, HogQLQuerySchema])`
- [`services/mcp/src/schema/query.ts:160-242`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/master/services/mcp/src/schema/query.ts#L160) — the three member schemas, each with `kind: z.literal(...)` at top level
- [`services/mcp/src/mcp.ts:443-453`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/master/services/mcp/src/mcp.ts#L443) — `this.server.registerTool(..., { inputSchema: tool.schema.shape, ... }, ...)` — passes the **shape** to the MCP SDK, not the schema
- [`services/mcp/package.json`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/master/services/mcp/package.json) — `zod ^4.3.6`, `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.29.0`
- [`services/mcp/tests/unit/query-run-schema.test.ts`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/master/services/mcp/tests/unit/query-run-schema.test.ts) — asserts payload #1 should succeed against `QueryRunInputSchema.safeParse(...)` directly. So `QueryRunInputSchema` is fine in isolation; the bug is downstream of `.shape` extraction.

### Hypothesized root cause

`registerTool` flattens the schema via `tool.schema.shape` and the MCP SDK reconstructs it with `z.object(shape)` for input validation. Reconstruction preserves the discriminated-union node by reference, but in Zod v4 the literal-detection table is built at `discriminatedUnion(...)` *construction* time. Whether that table survives the SDK's pipeline (Zod 4 → JSON Schema generation → AJV/Zod re-parse for inputs) is the most likely fault line.

A focused experiment: change

payload.body:
## Description

The Nuxt error tracking installation docs appear to use the wrong `sourcemaps` key for the PostHog project ID.

The docs currently show:

```ts
sourcemaps: {
  enabled: true,
  project: "<ph_project_id>",
  personalApiKey: "<ph_personal_api_key>",
  releaseName: "my-application",
  releaseVersion: "1.0.0"
}
```

But in the current `@posthog/nuxt` module, `projectId` is the field used for the PostHog project ID.

Relevant module code:

```ts
const projectId = sourcemapsConfig.projectId ?? sourcemapsConfig.envId
```
```ts
const releaseName = sourcemapsConfig.releaseName ?? sourcemapsConfig.project
```

`project` is deprecated and is used as a fallback for `releaseName`. Passing `project: "<ph_project_id>"` seems to set the release name, not `POSTHOG_CLI_PROJECT_ID`.

The same incorrect snippet also appears in the "Manual installation" portion of the Nuxt onboarding flow.

## Expected Change

```diff
 sourcemaps: {
   enabled: true,
-  project: "<ph_project_id>",
+  projectId: "<ph_project_id>",
   personalApiKey: "<ph_personal_api_key>",
   releaseName: "my-application",
   releaseVersion: "1.0.0"
 }
```

## Context

This discrepancy seems to have started after https://github.com/PostHog/posthog-js/pull/3076, where `envId` was renamed to `projectId`, and `project` was renamed to `releaseName`. In that PR, the README and example were updated to use `projectId`, but the [Nuxt error tracking docs](https://posthog.com/docs/error-tracking/installation/nuxt) and onboarding flow (`/project/<project>/onboarding/error_tracking?step=install`) still show `project`.

## Please describe

Images are too wide for the viewing pane in Outlook desktop, requiring horizontal scrolling preventing the viewing of the entire chart at once. The same emails render fine on mobile and in browser-based email clients, which use more forgiving image scaling. This is a problem for teams that distribute these reports to recipients who use Outlook desktop.

## How to reproduce

1. Subscribe an Outlook desktop recipient to a dashboard 
2. View the dashboard email in Outlook on a desktop

payload.author: andrewm4894
payload.body:
## Bug

The Tasks sandbox MCP client sends the header **`x-posthog-read-only`** (with a hyphen between `read` and `only`), but the MCP server reads **`x-posthog-readonly`** (no second hyphen). The two names never match, so the server's read-only enforcement never applies to sandbox-spawned MCP sessions.

The server has a query-param fallback (`?readonly=...`) but the sandbox does not set it, so there is no second path that would catch the mismatch.

## Code references

**Sender** — `products/tasks/backend/temporal/process_task/utils.py:363`
```python
{\"name\": \"x-posthog-read-only\", \"value\": str(read_only).lower()},
```

**Receiver** — `services/mcp/src/index.ts:333`
```ts
const readOnlyRaw = request.headers.get('x-posthog-readonly') || url.searchParams.get('readonly')
```

The sender line was introduced on 2026-03-09 in `2a68f4dd7750`, so the mismatch has been present for ~2 months.

## Impact

Two-directional risk:

1. **Today**: sandboxes spawned with MCP scopes that include any write capability still see those write tools, regardless of whether the caller intended a read-only session, because the read-only filter on the MCP side is silently bypassed.
2. **If the server is later fixed to also accept `x-posthog-read-only`**: any sandbox-launched workflow that relies on write tools (e.g. an agent harness that needs write-capable MCP tools) can suddenly lose them when the caller passes `read_only`-style scopes alongside the (now-honored) header.

## Suggested fix

Align both ends on a single header name. Recommend standardizing on the server's `x-posthog-readonly` (no second hyphen) since the MCP server is also consumed by external clients (Claude Desktop, etc.), and changing the wire format on the receiver side has a wider blast radius than fixing one Python sender.

Concretely:

- Update `_build_mcp_config` in `products/tasks/backend/temporal/process_task/utils.py` to emit `x-posthog-readonly`.
- Update related tests in `products/tasks/backend/temporal/process_task/tests/test_utils.py`.
- Audit any other internal callers (e.g. `services/agentsh`, eval harnesses) for the same name drift before landing.
- Add a lightweight integration test that exercises the wire format end-to-end so this kind of mismatch can't silently regress.

## Notes

Spotted while reviewing the Signals agent dev branch — the agent uses the standard sandbox MCP plumbing, which is how the issue surfaced, but the bug itself is independent of that work and affects every sandbox MCP consumer.
payload.title: bug(mcp): sandbox read-only header name mismatch — `x-posthog-read-only` vs `x-posthog-readonly`

### Feature request

## Is your feature request related to a problem?

When using marketing analytics, I would like to answer questions over time, e.g:

- *"Of the users I acquired through Google Ads in April, how much have they spent by July?"*
- *"Are users from campaign A still purchasing months later, while users from campaign B churn after the first order?"*
- *"Is my CAC justified once I look beyond the first purchase?"*

A customer has framed this request as *"Would it be possible in the future to have an LTV dashboard where we can track how new users perform over time and whether they continue making purchases?"*

Marketing analytics today is built around period rollups: cost in a period, conversions in a period, ROAS in a period. There's no concept of an acquired-user cohort that you can follow forward in time. ROAS, as currently computed (`conversion value in period / cost in period`), only ever reflects revenue that occurred in the same period as the spend, which materially undersells channels that take longer to pay back.

This is a gap for any customer with a multi-purchase business model: e-commerce with repeat purchases, subscriptions, marketplaces, B2B with expansion revenue.

### Feature request

## Is your feature request related to a problem?

A customer using marketing analytics with Google Ads set up "Order refunded" as a conversion goal and is reading "Cost per refunded order" as their indicator of how much they're paying to acquire users who later refund. The number they see is misleading.

Today, "Cost per X" is calculated at the period level: `total ad spend in the period/count of X events in the period`. For their 7-day window: €1700 spent / 10 refunds = €170 per refund.

The €1700 of ad spend in the numerator has no relationship to the campaigns that originally acquired the users who refunded this week. As a result, "Cost per refunded order" doesn't measure what the customer thinks it measures, and they're making decisions based on a number that conflates two unrelated periods.

The customer's own framing: *"if we acquire a user and pay for that acquisition, and they later refund an order, the cost of that refunded user should be based on how much we paid to acquire them, rather than the total weekly spend."*

The same mismatch shows up for any conversion goal that's structurally offset from acquisition: refunds, cancellations, churn, repeat purchases, etc. The current calculation is fine for sign-ups and first purchases (where the conversion happens shortly after the click), but breaks down everywhere else.

payload.author: dmarticus
payload.body:
## Summary

The cross-project feature flag copy capability has three gaps that together make it unusable from AI/MCP clients:

1. **MCP tool is end-to-end broken due to an auth-scope conflict.** `feature-flags-copy-flags-create` is enabled in `products/feature_flags/mcp/tools.yaml` with `feature_flag:write`, but `OrganizationFeatureFlagView` declares `scope_object = "INTERNAL"` (`posthog/api/organization_feature_flag.py:72`). `INTERNAL` rejects personal API key access at a higher gate than scope checks (`posthog/api/personal_api_key.py:201`), so the tool can never succeed regardless of granted scopes. Calls return `403 "This action does not support personal API key access"`.

2. **Organization ID is not resolved when the MCP tool builds the URL.** Observed call resolves to `POST /api/organizations/undefined/feature_flags/copy_flags/`. Even if (1) is fixed, the URL substitution for `{id}` is broken — separate bug from the auth gate.

3. **No skill exists for the workflow.** Agents have to wrangle the raw MCP tool, which (a) doesn't work today, and (b) wouldn't be discoverable even if it did. The "copy flag across projects" job-to-be-done has no entry in `products/feature_flags/skills/` or equivalent.

## Why this matters

Users today copy feature flags across projects manually. Internal product direction is moving toward treating projects as environments with resource sync between them — flag copy is the smallest, most concrete slice of that broader experience. Getting the AI-native path working unblocks the manual workaround for users and validates the pattern before broader resource sync lands.

Internal context (Slack, employees only): https://posthog.slack.com/archives/C07Q2U4BH4L/p1777476676713569 — summary: an earlier "environments" effort was rolled back; nearer term, the plan is to mask projects as environments with resource sync between them, with feature flag copy as the first concrete slice.

## Repro

Call the MCP tool against any project:

```
call feature-flags-copy-flags-create {
  \"feature_flag_key\": \"<any-key>\",
  \"from_project\": <source>,
  \"target_project_ids\": [<target>],
  \"copy_schedule\": false,
  \"disable_copied_flag\": true
}
```

Returns: `403 — This action does not support personal API key access`, with URL `/api/organizations/undefined/feature_flags/copy_flags/`.

## Proposed fixes

1. **Auth**: drop `INTERNAL` scope on `copy_flags` (or split the action onto a non-INTERNAL viewset). Require explicit `feature_flag:write` scope, gated by the existing `UserAccessControl` editor check that already runs (`organization_feature_flag.py:148-156`).
2. **Org ID resolution**: fix MCP URL substitution so `{id}` resolves to the user's org for org-scoped tools. Likely a generator/template bug — affects every org-scoped MCP tool, not just this one.
3. **Skill**: add a "copying-flags-across-projects" skill in `products/feature_flags/skills/` covering target project selection, disabled-by-default safety, scheduled-change handling, and the cohort remap behavior. Once (1) and (2) land.

## Out of scope

Broader project-as-environment / cross-resource sync work. This issue is scoped to making the existing `copy_flags` endpoint actually work for AI clients.
payload.title: Cross-project feature flag copy: MCP tool non-functional + missing skill

payload.author: alex-kozh
payload.body:
## Bug Description

After PR #54702 (merged 2026-04-22), the preflight `/_preflight/` endpoint unconditionally reports `kafka: false` for self-hosted instances, blocking the setup wizard "Validate implementation" step with "Queue · Kafka — Error" even when the Kafka (Redpanda) broker is healthy and serving the rest of the stack.

## Reproduce

1. Fresh hobby deploy on Ubuntu 24.04:
   ```bash
   /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/posthog/posthog/HEAD/bin/deploy-hobby)"
   ```
2. Open the instance in a browser and reach "Validate implementation".
3. Observe `Queue · Kafka — Error`, even though `docker compose ps kafka` is healthy and `rpk cluster health` reports `Healthy: true` with active consumer groups (capture, ingestion, clickhouse-ingestion, etc.).
4. `curl https://<instance>/_preflight | jq .kafka` returns `false`.

## Root Cause

PR #54702 ("feat: Setup kafka client routing via env vars") removed the `is_kafka_connected()` import and call from `posthog/views.py`:

```diff
-from posthog.health import is_clickhouse_connected, is_kafka_connected
+from posthog.health import is_clickhouse_connected

-"kafka": is_cloud() or is_kafka_connected() or settings.TEST,
+"kafka": is_cloud() or settings.TEST,
```

It also deleted `is_kafka_connected` from `posthog/health.py`. The PR description explains the motivation:

> "Removed the kafka health check as I dont think it makes sense given a multi-kafka setup - also we wouldnt want the app to actually go unhealthy in that situation"

That reasoning applies to cloud / multi-Warpstream-cluster deployments. On self-hosted, where `is_cloud()` is always `False` and `settings.TEST` is `False`, the preflight `kafka` field is now wired to a constant `False`, which the frontend (`PreflightCheck`) renders as Error and which blocks `live` mode users from completing setup.

The frontend check is in `chunk-LZVU2JOU.js` (compiled):
```javascript
{id:"kafka", name:"Queue · Kafka", status: e?.kafka ? "validated" : "error"}
```

## Workaround

Choose "Just experimenting" mode instead of "Live implementation" — the wizard's experimentation mode allows Continue regardless of preflight errors. Functionally equivalent thereafter.

## Suggested Fix

Restore an actual broker probe for self-hosted, e.g. guard the cloud / multi-cluster behavior:

```python
"kafka": is_cloud() or is_kafka_connected_for_self_host() or settings.TEST,
```

…where `is_kafka_connected_for_self_host()` does a single-broker reachability check using the existing `KAFKA_HOSTS` setting (similar to the removed `is_kafka_connected`), and is bypassed on cloud.

## Environment

- PostHog: `posthog/posthog:latest` (commit per `git_commit_short` from `instance_status` — date 2026-04-30)
- Deployment: hobby (`bin/deploy-hobby latest <domain>`)
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS, Docker Compose v2
- Broker: Redpanda v25.1.9 as `kafka` service (per `docker-compose.base.yml`)

## Related

- Plugin server preflight previously had a similar regression — fixed by #31368.
payload.title: Preflight wizard reports "Queue · Kafka — Error" on self-hosted (regression from #54702)

## Summary

Customer Analytics should show the communication history for each account, regardless of where the interaction happened.

This is the parent issue for ingesting, linking, and presenting customer communications in Customer Analytics. Channel-specific implementation details belong in child issues.

The goal is a consistent account-level history covering email, support conversations, Slack and Teams threads, GitHub discussions, meetings, and future communication sources.

## Architectural direction

- **Conversations owns communications.** Conversations is the canonical hub for communication threads and messages, including communication that is not a support ticket.
- **Customer Analytics owns account context.** Customer Analytics matches communications to accounts and presents them through account views.
- **`Comment` can hold canonical message content.** Channel-specific envelope data and thread identity should live in typed Conversations models rather than only in `Comment.item_context`.
- **Tickets are a specialized workflow.** A support Ticket can be associated with a communication thread, but ordinary customer communication should not need to become a Ticket.
- **Products communicate through facades.** Customer Analytics should not query Conversations ORM models directly, and Conversations should not depend on Customer Analytics account tables.
- **Account links use stable external keys.** A communication may link to more than one account when its participants span several customer organizations.

## Shared requirements

Every channel integration should address:

- tenant isolation and access control for message content
- provider authentication and source verification
- idempotent ingestion and stable external identifiers
- thread continuity and duplicate suppression
- participant normalization and optional person resolution
- account matching through group keys, known addresses, domains, or channel-specific configuration
- source timestamps rather than ingestion timestamps
- deletion, disconnect, and retention behavior
- safe telemetry that excludes message bodies and customer identifiers
- channel-specific failures without disrupting other communication sources

## Workstreams

- [x] #76054
- [x] #74016
- [x] #76088
- [x] #74027
- [x] #74029

Add channel-specific issues here as the communication hub expands.

## Account experience

An account should eventually provide a chronological view of its customer interactions with enough source context to understand where each interaction happened.

The initial surfaces can remain channel-specific, such as separate Meetings, Support tickets, and Email threads tabs. A unified timeline can follow after the underlying communication contracts stabilize.

## Open decisions

- When should channel-specific thread models converge on a more general Conversation model?
- How should existing email-sourced support Tickets migrate to or link with canonical EmailThread records?
- Which account roles can read full message bodies versus summaries and metadata?
- How should account links be recalculated when account matching configuration or person-group membership changes?
- Which communication types belong in a future unified timeline, and which should remain separate account tabs?

## Goal

Create one source of truth for customer feature requests in Customer Analytics. Let users record demand in customer language and break it down by account and product.

PostHog is moving off Vitally. The replacement must preserve historical context and support a controlled cutover.

## Ideal end state

- Customer-facing teams create and maintain requests in Customer Analytics.
- A shared request can link to multiple accounts.
- Each account keeps its own quote, source, summary, and request date.
- Requests use a maintained product-area vocabulary.
- Users can search, filter, archive, and inspect history.
- Valid GitHub issues can update customer-facing status through an explicit mapping.
- Historical Vitally records remain available, including unresolved account references.
- Product teams can report by account, product, status, priority, and time, then drill into the underlying requests.
- Viewer and editor permissions protect customer evidence and internal links.
- Migration and GitHub failures are visible, recoverable, and auditable.

## Parent user stories

- As a customer-facing teammate, I can record a request in customer language and connect it to affected accounts and products, so product teams can understand demand.
- As an account owner, I can record each account's evidence for a shared request, so customer context remains distinct.
- As a product manager, I can break requests down by account and product and open the underlying records, so I can prioritize with evidence.
- As a customer-facing teammate, I can link an engineering issue and trust completed work to update customer-facing status.
- As a migration owner, I can move Vitally history without losing, hiding, or duplicating records.

## Minimal valuable feature

The first usable release is #81883.

An editor can create a request with a customer-facing title and description, one account link, and one or more product areas. A viewer can find and inspect it after refresh.

This slice includes the minimum interface, API, domain rule, persistence, permissions, and error states. It does not require later groundwork issues before users receive value.

## Scope

- A first-class feature request capability in Customer Analytics.
- Shared requests, account links, account-specific evidence, product areas, lifecycle, and history.
- Vitally migration and reconciliation.
- GitHub issue status synchronization and reliability.
- Account and product reporting with drill-down.

## Non-goals

These require separate approval after the planned release:

- Voting or upvotes.
- MRR-weighted scoring.
- Generic custom fields.
- Comments and notifications.
- Automated duplicate merging.
- Pull-request synchronization.
- Destructive source cleanup.

## Decisions already recorded

1. Customer Analytics owns the customer-facing title and description. A linked GitHub issue does not overwrite them.
2. A linked GitHub issue can update request status. #81882 must define the exact mapping and manual-override behavior.
3. Work ships as additive vertical slices. The first implementation issue must deliver a usable end-to-end story.
4. Requests support multiple team-maintained product areas.
5. Customer-facing means internal teammates who work with customers. Public or customer-visible request views are out of scope.
6. Request merging, consolidation, and automatic duplicate detection are out of scope.

## Verified source state

The July 30, 2026 snapshot contains:

- 383 records and 449 account links.
- 36 requests linked to more than one account.
- Up to 7 accounts on one request.
- No request with zero account links.
- 363 records with a status, which means 20 missing statuses, not 19.
- 35 priority keys, including 1 empty value.
- 88 quarterly-planning keys, including 4 empty values.
- One malformed status stored as the literal 11-character value `"requested"`.

URL fields need classification rather than direct copying:

- `signalUrl`: 146 BuildBetter, 34 Slack, 4 Zendesk, 1 unparsed,

payload.body:
## Background

With per-condition aggregation ("mixed targeting") now shipped, the top-level **Match by** selector — User / Device / Group / User & Group — is largely redundant. User, Group, and User & Group are all forms of property-based targeting; only Device is a meaningfully different code path because it changes `bucketing_identifier`.

## Goal

Replace the four-card top-level selector with **two cards**:

- **Properties** — target by user or group property filters. Each condition set picks its own scope independently.
- **Device** — stable assignment per device (good for anonymous users).

Within each condition set, the **Target by** selector is always-on (when the project has group types) and offers **Users plus every group type** in the project. This is strictly more powerful than today's UI, which funnels mixed-mode flags through a single `mixedGroupTypeIndex`.

## Mockup

**Top-level selector**

| Properties (selected) | Device |
| --- | --- |
| Target by user or group property filters. Each condition picks its own targeting type. | Stable assignment per device. Good fit for experiments on anonymous users. |

**Per-condition Target by select** — different scopes per condition fully supported:

> Condition set 1 — `Target by [Users ▾]` — `email contains "@posthog.com"` — 20%
> Condition set 2 — `Target by [Organizations ▾]` — `plan = "enterprise"` — 100%
> Condition set 3 — `Target by [Projects ▾]` — `workspace_count > 5` — 50%

## Plan

### PR 1 — v2 UI behind `feature-flag-mixed-targeting` (#57007, in review)

The mixed-targeting flag is repurposed as the v2 gate — it was always v1 of "let users pick scope per condition", and v2 is just polish (collapse 4 cards to 2, surface the per-condition picker by default, list every group type instead of just one). Anyone with the flag enabled gets the new UI automatically.

- New v2 UI rendered when `feature-flag-mixed-targeting` is on
- Legacy 4-card UI rendered when off
- Read path normalizes per-condition `aggregation_group_type_index`, falling back to flag-level for legacy flags
- Write path persists per-condition + flag-level `null`
- Legacy "User & Group" card and per-condition picker (only reachable with the flag) deleted in this PR

### PR 2 — delete legacy paths once v2 is GA

After ramping `feature-flag-mixed-targeting` to 100%:

- Delete `mixedGroupTypeIndex`, `isMixedTargeting`, the legacy 3-card selector, `switchToMixedTargeting`, `setIsMixedTargeting`, `hasMixedAggregations`
- Remove `_is_mixed_targeting_enabled()` gate at `posthog/api/feature_flag.py:948` — v2 makes mixed targeting the only mode
- The legacy `FeatureFlagReleaseConditions.tsx` (non-collapsible) gets the same treatment or is just removed if no callers remain

### PR 3 — docs and copy sweep

Update copy across `docs/`, in-product strings, and the description-enrichment logic from a66f2f5b21d. Help articles and the posthog.com blog post live outside this repo and need to be coordinated with content/support.

Files to grep:
- `docs/` for "Match by", "User & Group"
- `frontend/src/scenes/feature-flags/` and `products/feature_flags/frontend/`
- `posthog/api/feature_flag.py` description-enrichment

## Migration notes

- **Read path:** legacy flags with `aggregation_group_type_index = 2` and no per-condition values are rendered as if every condition has `aggregation_group_type_index = 2`. The "Target by" select pre-selects the right scope, no surprise.
- **Write path:** v2 always writes per-condition and clears the flag-level field.
- **Backend:** the Rust evaluator already handles per-condition aggregation and falls back to flag-level. No backend changes needed for PR 1; PR 2 removes the validator gate.
- **No groups in project:** "Target by" hidden, UI collapses to a single property filter list per condition (visually unchanged from today's "User" mode).
- **Device → Properties:** existing logic in `setAggregationGroupTypeIndex` clears stale group state when switching scopes. Reused.

payload.body:
## **Is your feature request related to a problem?**

**Yes: Improper customer attribution during internal email forwarding.**

When a team member receives a customer inquiry in their personal inbox and forwards it to our PostHog support address, PostHog attributes the ticket to the **employee (the forwarder)** rather than the **customer**.

This creates several points of friction:

* **Misaligned Identity:** Tickets are linked to internal users, breaking customer history and CRM integrity.  
* **Incorrect Notifications:** Automated responses (like "We received your request") are sent to the staff member instead of the client.  
* **Manual Toil:** Support agents must manually edit the requester on every forwarded ticket to ensure the customer receives the eventual resolution.

## **Describe the solution you'd like**

PostHog should implement logic to detect forwarded emails and automatically attribute the ticket to the **original customer** instead of the forwarder.

**Proposed Logic:**

1. **Trigger on Internal Domain:** If an email is sent to support from an internal address (e.g., @ourdomain.com), the system should check for a forwarded payload.  
2. **Body/Header Parsing:** Scan the top of the email body for standard "Forwarded message" headers.  
3. **Customer Attribution:** Extract the customer's email address from the From: line of the forwarded section and set **that address** as the primary requester of the ticket.

## **Describe alternatives you've considered**

* **Manual Re-assignment:** Agents manually updating the "Requested by" field. This is the current workaround but is highly inefficient as we scale.  
* **Email Redirects:** Training the whole company to use "Redirect" instead of "Forward," which is technically difficult as standard mail clients (Gmail/Outlook mobile) often don't support it easily.

## **Additional context**

Standard help desk tools (Zendesk, Front, etc.) handle this automatically by parsing the message body. This allows our Sales and Success teams to seamlessly hand off conversations to Support without losing the customer's identity in the process.

**Example of content to be parsed:**

\---------- Forwarded message \--------- From: **Customer Name [customer@example.com](mailto:customer@example.com)** Date: Wed, Apr 29, 2026 at 10:00 AM Subject: Question about my subscription To: Employee [employee@ourdomain.com](mailto:employee@ourdomain.com)

The PostHog MCP exposes operations through a single `mcp__posthog__exec` entry point that takes a CLI-style command string, e.g.:

## Summary

The PostHog wizard reported a Next.js dashboard integration as complete, but the deployed app in a local kind/Kubernetes environment did not emit events until we manually rebuilt/redeployed the dashboard image and passed the PostHog env values through both the build-time and runtime paths.

This made the wizard sit at "waiting for events" even though the local source integration looked complete.

## What happened

The wizard added PostHog client code to the local dashboard source, including the Next.js `instrumentation-client.ts` integration. However, the active dashboard was running from a previously built Docker image in kind, so the deployed dashboard did not contain the new PostHog bundle.

For this Next.js dashboard, `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST` also needed to be present during `docker build`, not only at container runtime. The kind deployment additionally needed those values passed through Helm `extraEnv` for server-side PostHog usage.

There was also a deployment-specific routing issue: `/ingest` requests were intercepted by the dashboard auth proxy and redirected to login instead of being forwarded to PostHog, so even bundled client events could fail to reach PostHog.

## Issues encountered

- Wizard verified local source changes, but not the actually deployed dashboard image.
- Wizard did not surface that `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_*` values must be available at Docker build time for Next.js client bundles.
- Wizard did not account for Helm/runtime env injection needed by the deployed app.
- Wizard verification waited for events without identifying that `/ingest` was being redirected by app auth middleware.
- A Helm arg generation bug was easy to introduce: optional env vars emitted as fixed `extraEnv[0]` / `extraEnv[1]` indexes can create a sparse array if one value is absent, producing an invalid Kubernetes env entry.

## Suggested improvements

- Detect when the app appears to be running from Docker, kind, or Kubernetes, and warn that source changes require image rebuild, image load, and rollout.
- For Next.js, explicitly validate whether `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_*` values are present during build, not just runtime.
- Add a deployment checklist for common paths:
  - Docker build args
  - container runtime env
  - Helm `extraEnv`
  - Kubernetes rollout restart/status
- During verification, test the deployed app's ingestion path directly, for example `/ingest/capture/`, and report redirects/auth failures clearly.
- Detect auth middleware/proxy rewrites that block PostHog ingest routes.
- When generating Helm examples, use contiguous `extraEnv` indexes when optional env vars are omitted.
- Avoid reporting the setup as complete until the wizard confirms an event from the deployed app, not just local code presence.

## Expected behavior

The wizard should distinguish between "PostHog code was added locally" and "the deployed application is sending events." If deployment steps are required, it should either perform them when possible or provide explicit commands and validation checks.
payload.title: Improve wizard validation for containerized Next.js/kind deployments

## Bug description

When a user asks Max AI to edit values inside a Hog function's filter configuration, the agent occasionally edits the **field description / UI label** instead of the actual field value. The result is that the Hog function configuration UI gets visibly mutated (labels rewritten) rather than the underlying filter values being changed.

The issue is inconsistent — in the same trace, GPT-4.1 produced the bug while Sonnet 4.5 handled the same request correctly on a follow-up call.

The `create_hog_function_filters` tool is part of a legacy agent implementation that still runs on GPT-4.1, and the subagent response does not use structured output, so the model has room to write the value into the wrong field of the schema.

## How to reproduce

1. Open a Hog function (destination or source) configuration.
2. Ask Max AI to edit a filter value (e.g. "change the filter value for X to Y").
3. Observe that, intermittently, the field's label/description is rewritten instead of the value.

Note: not 100% reproducible — depends on which model the subagent ends up running and how it interprets the schema on a given call.

## Additional context

From: https://posthoghelp.zendesk.com/agent/tickets/47775 (moved to PostHog: https://us.posthog.com/project/2/support/tickets/57261)

Proper fix is part of the broader migration of legacy agent tools to MCP tools with structured output enforced. Short-term mitigations worth considering if the migration takes a while: enforce structured output on the existing GPT-4.1 subagent call, or add input validation that rejects writes to label/description fields.
payload.title: Bug: Max AI edits Hog function field labels instead of field values

payload.author: kuishou68
payload.body:
In `posthog/caching/utils.py`, the `ThresholdMode` enum defines a `LEGACY = "legacy"` member, but `staleness_threshold_map` only includes entries for `ThresholdMode.DEFAULT`, `ThresholdMode.LAZY`, and `ThresholdMode.AI`. Passing `mode=ThresholdMode.LEGACY` to `cache_target_age()` or `is_stale()` will raise a `KeyError` at runtime.

## Code

```python
class ThresholdMode(Enum):
    LEGACY = "legacy"
    DEFAULT = "default"
    LAZY = "lazy"
    AI = "ai"

staleness_threshold_map: dict[ThresholdMode, dict[Optional[str], timedelta]] = {
    ThresholdMode.DEFAULT: { ... },
    ThresholdMode.LAZY: { ... },
    ThresholdMode.AI: { ... },
    # ThresholdMode.LEGACY is missing!
}
```

Then in `cache_target_age()`:
```python
def cache_target_age(interval, last_refresh, mode=ThresholdMode.DEFAULT):
    if interval not in staleness_threshold_map[mode]:  # KeyError if mode=LEGACY
        return None
```

## Fix

Either add `ThresholdMode.LEGACY` to `staleness_threshold_map` with appropriate thresholds, or remove the unused `LEGACY` enum member to avoid confusion and future misuse.

Signed-off-by: cocoon <54054995+kuishou68@users.noreply.github.com>
payload.title: fix: ThresholdMode.LEGACY is defined but missing from staleness_threshold_map, causing KeyError

right now cutomer's with jobs that exceed the CH timeout even once are penalized with their temporal schedule being paused.

this is too aggressive. transient timeouts are more common than we'd like and we shouldn't make that our customer's problem to solve. so we are making the new policy 5 consecutive timeouts. in the most extreme case (15 min syncs) this means a matview would have to timeout consistently over a 75 minute window, giving CH at least a moderate window of time to recover from load spikes.

payload.author: andrewjmcgehee
payload.body:
out temporal overlap policy is skip which means that matview schedules that exceed their schedule frequency (say a 30 minute materialization scheduled to run every 15 mins) doesn't get preempted but instead skips the next scheduled run until it completes.

this incentivizes the wrong behavior from our customers. you shouldn't schedule something to sync every 15 mins if it cannot complete in 15 mins. so we are changing the overlap policy to "cancel other" which means new runs will cancel older ones. 

this has the added benefit that customers job run logs should appear more "correct" now as well with jobs run close to every interval but with ones that exceed the time allotted marked as preempted.
payload.title: fix starved temporal queues with better overlap policy

payload.author: haacked
payload.body:
## Problem

The `create-feature-flag` and `update-feature-flag` MCP tools don't expose
`is_remote_configuration`, so agents can't create or convert a flag into
Remote Config mode through the MCP.

- `create-feature-flag` always creates flags with `is_remote_configuration: false`.
- `update-feature-flag` can't flip an existing flag into Remote Config mode.
- The only workaround is a manual toggle in the PostHog UI, which defeats
  the point of managing flags through the MCP.

The field is read-exposed: `feature-flag-get-definition` returns
`is_remote_configuration: <bool>` on any flag. It's settable in the UI and
the Django serializer (`posthog/api/feature_flag.py`) lists it among
writable fields. It's just unreachable through the MCP write tools.

## Where it lives

`products/feature_flags/mcp/tools.yaml` has explicit `include_params`
allowlists for both tools that omit `is_remote_configuration`:

```yaml
create-feature-flag:
    operation: feature_flags_create
    ...
    include_params:
        - key
        - name
        - filters
        - active
        - tags
        - evaluation_contexts

update-feature-flag:
    operation: feature_flags_partial_update
    ...
    include_params:
        - key
        - name
        - filters
        - active
        - tags
        - evaluation_contexts
```

The generated `services/mcp/src/tools/generated/feature_flags.ts` only
copies those six fields into the request body, so `is_remote_configuration`
never reaches the API even if a caller supplies it.

## Suggested fix

Add `is_remote_configuration` to both `include_params` lists in
`tools.yaml` and regenerate. The underlying `FeatureFlagsCreateBody` /
`FeatureFlagsPartialUpdateBody` schemas generated from the OpenAPI spec
already include the field, so no serializer or API changes should be
needed.

Remote Config flags also require a payload — worth deciding whether to
surface `has_encrypted_payloads` and payload fields in the same pass, or
document that as a follow-up.
payload.title: MCP `create-feature-flag` and `update-feature-flag` can't set `is_remote_configuration`

### Feature request

## Is your feature request related to a problem?

When using PostHog AI in the sidebar to generate queries for an insight already in context, the agent can prompt the user to Accept and run before the sidebar query has fully updated or before the new SQL has been validated.

This creates a confusing experience: the user is asked to approve a query change optimistically, then the sidebar may update and show no results or an invalid outcome afterward. It can feel like the system is requesting confirmation before knowing whether the query actually works.

In conversations where the agent is refining the query multiple times, this also adds friction. Instead of feeling iterative and conversational, the workflow becomes repetitive and interrupts momentum.

## Describe the solution you'd like

The AI should only surface Accept and run once the proposed SQL has been validated and is ready for the user to apply.

A smoother experience would be for intermediate SQL revisions to run silently in the background so the agent can test results, refine the query, and continue iterating without repeated approval prompts. Once the agent has confidence that the final version works, it should present the completed query for a single approval and execution step.

This would reduce confusion, prevent premature prompts, and make the interaction feel faster and more aligned with an AI assistant workflow.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

- Keep the current approval flow, but only require approval when the SQL meaningfully changes rather than on every minor revision.
- Add an “auto-run while iterating” mode users can enable for a session.
- Batch revisions so multiple query updates happen behind the scenes, then present the latest version for approval.
- Allow users to opt into trusting the AI for temporary exploratory runs, while still requiring approval for saved or production insights.

## Additional context

This issue is most noticeable during longer back-and-forth chats where the AI needs several attempts to get the SQL right. Requiring repeated clicks to accept/run makes experimentation feel slower than it should. Reducing approval prompts during iteration would significantly improve usability.

Requested by Sandy: https://posthog.slack.com/archives/C06NZEZ7V3Q/p1777051588518959

### Debug info

```shell

```
payload.title: feat(phai): Reduce repeated “Accept and run” prompts during AI SQL query iteration

payload.author: matheus-vb
payload.body:
## Problem

A feature flags customer recently needed a small number of their users throttled because those users were generating disproportionate request volume. The customer identified them by `distinct_id`. We had no way to express that directly, so we resolved each `distinct_id` to a source IP and hardcoded the IP into Envoy's global rate limit configuration. This was done in charts#9712 (shadow) and charts#9720 (enforce).

This approach has several problems. We end up limiting IPs when the customer asked us to limit users, which is the wrong identifier because IPs rotate through NATs, mobile carriers, and shared CGNAT, so the rule hits bystanders and misses the real offenders. Envoy sees only an IP and a path, so the rule cannot be scoped to a single team. Every new entry requires a PostHog engineer to edit YAML in `charts/` and wait on ArgoCD, which does not scale to many users or many customers. The rule tree on the shared ratelimit service also grows with each unrelated customer request.

## Proposed solution

Give each team a first class list of `distinct_id`s to block or throttle at the feature flags service itself. Customers manage the list through the normal team settings API. The list is shipped to the Rust feature flags service via the same HyperCache mechanism already used to distribute flag definitions, so the hot path only does an in memory lookup.

## High level design

1. Backend model. Add a `TeamFeatureFlagRateLimitConfig` Team extension (per the pattern in `posthog/models/team/README.md`) with three fields: a blocklist of distinct ids, an optional per id rate spec for soft throttling, and an enforcement mode (`off`, `shadow`, `enforce`). Expose the config on the existing Team API with admin level field access control.
2. Distribution. A Celery task pushes the config to a new HyperCache namespace keyed by team api token on every change, mirroring how `flag_definitions_hypercache` already works. Redis plus S3 backed, roughly 30 second propagation.
3. Enforcement. The Rust feature flags service loads each team's config from HyperCache into a `HashSet` (blocklist) and a `HashMap` of `governor::Quota` (rate limits). The check runs in `handler::process_request` immediately after `cookieless::handle_distinct_id` resolves the final identifier and before flag fetch and evaluation. Blocked requests return an empty flags response with a `rate_limited=true` marker so SDKs degrade gracefully. Throttled requests reuse the existing `FlagsRateLimiter` plumbing.
4. Shadow mode. `shadow` evaluates the rule and emits metrics and a canonical log field but still returns real flag results. Each team can validate its list before flipping to `enforce`, without a global environment variable toggle.
5. Observability. New metric `flags_distinct_id_limit_evaluated_total{team_id, mode, action}` for allow, shadow block, enforced block, shadow throttle, enforced throttle. Add a panel to `feature-flags-general.json`. The canonical log gains a `distinct_id_rate_limited` field so Loki queries can answer whether a specific request was blocked by a team rule.
6. Failure mode. If HyperCache is unavailable, fail open and allow the request, matching the existing billing limiter posture.

## Performance

The hot path per request is one `DashMap` read on the HyperCache reader, one `HashSet::contains`, and optionally one `governor::check_key` if the id is also soft throttled. No Redis or Postgres call per request. Config refresh happens on a background interval.

## Migration

Ship with `mode=off` as the default so no team is affected at deploy time. For the currently hardcoded customer, populate their config with the distinct ids that motivated the original IP rule, run in `shadow` for roughly 24 hours and compare against the Envoy counter in Grafana, then flip to `enforce` and revert the IP rule in charts.
payload.title: Team managed throttling of feature flag requests by distinct_id

payload.author: dankhan
payload.body:
### Bug Description

This is a weird one that's taken me a long time to track down, and unlikely to be able to give you solid reproduction easily.

In my repo when I was running into intermittent http serving errors of the built code.  The only thing I could track it down to in my build pipeline is that after running `npm run build` on my repo, I followed it by the following posthog/@cli commands to inject the code to generate sourcemaps and upload them onto the server:

```bash
npm run build && \
npx @posthog/cli@latest sourcemap inject --directory /app/.output/public && \
npx @posthog/cli@latest sourcemap upload --directory /app/.output/public
```

But when looking at the http serving errors I had, the served file size was 420 bytes and the output content was truncated, but looking at the built files inside the container it should have been serving, this was 780 bytes on disk and no truncation of content.

The only thing I could finally track down to is the posthog/@cli obviously injects code into each built chunk so it can associate each chunk with the right sourcemap via the posthog cli call.

But nitro serves built files from it's own `output/server/chunks/nitro/nitro.mjs` script and this script caches the built assets and logs every file size, and etag (file hash) after the build step has completed as part of it's server build tools.

When serving any file nitro uses this file and the cached asset map within it to determine the size and etag of the file it serves up:

```
const assets = {
"/_nuxt/B3nvVOrL.js": {
    "type": "application/json",
    "etag": "\"74fa-VKz0d0mFbYGP22ECRFyNDEwAXEQ=\"",
    "mtime": "2026-04-22T21:18:39.023Z",
    "size": 420,
    "path": "../public/_nuxt/B3nvVOrL.js.map"
  },
}
```

It lists every served up built asset in here in this cached array.  

But `posthog/@cli sourcemap inject` transforms every chunk to add it's own instrumentation code and comments, but crucially, it doesn't rewrite the nitro asset map so those cached file sizes and etags are no longer consistent.  So, posthog/@cli rewrites the file contents (etag changes) and the file size (size changes), but nitro serves up the etag and file size in this cached asset map which no longer match the file size and contents, hence it serves a weirdly truncated file some times as it cuts off in my case at 420 bytes not the full 750 bytes of the newly mutated file (which was originally 420 bytes before posthog instrumentation).  Doesn't happen to all my files served up by nitro but at least one and it feels like a weird edge case.

## How to reproduce

1. build a starter vuejs/nuxt project which bundles in nitro
2. run `npm run build` and inspect the generated `output/server/chunks/nitro/nitro.mjs` asset map
3. run `npx @posthog/cli@latest sourcemap inject --directory /app/.output/public`
4. inspect the sizes of the chunk files where posthog added instrumentation
5. compare them to the sizes in the cached asset map - they will be wrong

Not sure if this is directly a `posthog/@cli` bug or a nitro bug, but it's a weird interaction with both since nitro assumes the post-build generated files won't be mutated and posthog/cli specifically mutates them afterwards, but doesn't complete this mutation across other dependent files, which is why I am reporting it here.

My temporary workaround is to add a build script in my build pipeline after `posthog/@cli` has mutated nitro chunk files, to rewrite the asset map in `nitro.mjs`, by re-inspecting the mutated chunk files sizes and generate new hashes to make new etags and rewrite the files sizes.  Hopefully this fixes this issue s a temporary workaround.
payload.title: Posthog/@cli doesn't rewrite nitro asset maps when mutating nitro chunk files for sourcemap injection

payload.author: rieger-jared
payload.body:
### Feature request

## Is your feature request related to a problem?

PostHog’s data warehouse integrations require PostHog to establish network access to the underlying datasource. In practice, this often means exposing a database or service to inbound internet traffic.

Common approaches like IP allowlisting still rely on public exposure and correct network configuration to remain secure. This increases operational overhead and introduces risk, particularly in environments where static IPs are unavailable or difficult to manage.

From a security perspective, requiring inbound access is not ideal when a more restrictive model could avoid exposure entirely.

## Describe the solution you’d like

Add support for a private network connector for data warehouse sources.

This would be a lightweight, customer ran agent that establishes an outbound authenticated connection to PostHog. PostHog could then use this connection to access private datasources for its existing pull based sync jobs, without requiring those datasources to be publicly exposed.

In the source configuration UI, users could select this connector as the network path, while keeping the current warehouse sync model unchanged.

## Describe alternatives you’ve considered

* Publicly exposing the datasource so PostHog can connect directly
* IP allowlisting (still requires inbound exposure and configuration)
* SSH tunneling
* Building and maintaining a custom proxy/tunnel
* Migrating to infrastructure that better supports network controls

payload.author: charlesvien
payload.body: ### Context Raised in Slack. Users who prefer Plan Mode as their default frequently kick off skills as new tasks. Skills almost never benefit from running in Plan Mode, they are meant to execute, not plan. ### Problem When a user is in Plan Mode and triggers a skill (e.g. `/commit`, `/simplify`), the skill runs in Plan Mode too. This means the skill describes what it *would* do instead of actually doing it, which is almost never the desired behavior. ### Expected behavior Two possible improvements (not mutually exclusive): 1. **Prompt on discrepancy**: When a skill is triggered while in Plan Mode, show a prompt like: *"It looks like you're running a skill in Plan Mode. Did you mean to execute the skill?"* with options to continue in Plan Mode or switch to execution. 2. **Auto-exit Plan Mode for skills** (preferred): Automatically exit Plan Mode when a skill is invoked, so the skill executes normally. This could be controlled by a setting (e.g. `autoExitPlanModeForSkills: true`) for users who want the current behavior.
payload.title: Auto-exit Plan Mode when executing a skill
